clinicalPearls: A qualitative fibrinogen defect in which a structurally abnormal molecule is produced, so functional fibrinogen is low while immunological (antigen) levels are near normal
The clinical picture is heterogeneous: many carriers are asymptomatic, some bleed, and a notable minority have a paradoxical tendency to thrombosis
The hallmark laboratory pattern is a discrepancy between a reduced Clauss (functional) fibrinogen and a normal or near-normal antigen level
Prolonged thrombin time and reptilase time are characteristic, reflecting defective fibrin polymerisation
Congenital forms arise from variants in the fibrinogen genes (FGA, FGB, FGG); acquired forms occur with liver disease and some malignancies
Certain variants are strongly linked to venous thrombosis, so a bleeding-only mindset can be misleading
Management is guided by the individual and family phenotype, using fibrinogen replacement for bleeding and anticoagulation for thrombotic presentations rather than a fixed protocol
reference.pathophysiology: Dysfibrinogenaemia results from an amino-acid substitution or other structural abnormality in one of the fibrinogen chains, yielding a molecule that is synthesised and secreted but functions abnormally. Depending on the site of the defect, fibrin monomer polymerisation, fibrinopeptide release, cross-linking, or interaction with thrombin and plasmin is impaired. Some variants produce a fibrin clot that resists fibrinolysis or fails to bind thrombin normally, explaining the paradoxical thrombotic phenotype, while others yield a friable clot that bleeds. Acquired dysfibrinogenaemia typically reflects abnormal glycosylation of fibrinogen in hepatic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Liver disease causing acquired fibrinogen dysfunction
Direct thrombin inhibitor or heparin effect prolonging the thrombin time
Other inherited thrombophilias when thrombosis predominates
Factor XIII deficiency when clot instability is prominent
additionalInvestigations: Clauss functional fibrinogen assay compared with fibrinogen antigen to demonstrate a functional-to-antigen discrepancy
Thrombin time and reptilase time to detect impaired fibrin polymerisation
Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time as screening tests
Fibrinogen gene sequencing (FGA, FGB, FGG) to confirm a congenital variant
Liver function tests to identify an acquired hepatic cause
Thrombophilia workup and imaging when a thrombotic event has occurred
redFlags: Unexplained venous or arterial thrombosis in a patient labelled as having a bleeding disorder
Severe or postoperative bleeding out of proportion to the platelet count
Pregnancy loss or thrombotic complications during pregnancy
Rapidly falling fibrinogen suggesting acquired consumption or hepatic decompensation
reference.prognosis: Outlook is variable and phenotype-dependent; many individuals live normally, whereas those with bleeding-prone or thrombosis-prone variants face event-related morbidity. Recognising the specific familial phenotype allows tailored prophylaxis and generally favourable long-term outcomes.
pitfalls: Assuming a low fibrinogen means bleeding risk when the variant is actually prothrombotic
Measuring only antigen and missing the functional deficit
Overlooking acquired dysfibrinogenaemia in a patient with liver disease
Failing to relate the laboratory abnormality to the individual and family bleeding or thrombotic history
references: Hoffman: Hematology - Basic Principles and Practice
management: Characterise the familial phenotype (asymptomatic, bleeding-prone or thrombosis-prone) and tailor prophylaxis to it rather than treating all carriers alike
Treat bleeding episodes and cover surgery or delivery with fibrinogen concentrate (or cryoprecipitate where concentrate is unavailable), guided by functional fibrinogen and clinical response
Use an antifibrinolytic such as tranexamic acid for mucosal or minor bleeding
Anticoagulate thrombosis-prone variants presenting with venous thromboembolism, and consider extended anticoagulation given the paradoxical prothrombotic tendency
In acquired dysfibrinogenaemia, treat the underlying hepatic disease or malignancy driving abnormal fibrinogen glycosylation
Offer genetic counselling and family testing for congenital FGA, FGB or FGG variants, and educate on signs of both bleeding and thrombosis
Escalate major bleeding or recurrent thrombosis to a specialist haemostasis centre for individualised management
